title: Tzedakah and the Ladder of Giving
hookLine: every stream teaches giving, kindness and justice
carry: tzedakah: giving that sets the world right

cards: Two families on the same street could argue for an hour about Shabbat, or prayer, or who counts in a minyan. One keeps every detail of Jewish law; the other keeps almost none.
Yet on both kitchen windowsills sits the same small tin box with a slot in the lid. Coins go in before candles are lit on Friday, or when a child finds a quarter in the couch. The box doesn't argue.
It just fills up. Today is about the ground the streams stand on together, and the box is a good place to start.

teach.b: Shared ethics. Three words, and one ladder. First, tzedakah, the giving that fills the box.
It's usually translated charity, but some teachers hear in it tzedek, justice: giving is not a favor to the poor, it is part of setting the world right.
Second, chesed, kindness beyond what anyone owes. Simeon the Just, in the Mishnah, says the world stands on three things: Torah, worship, and acts of loving-kindness. Third, justice itself.
The Torah doubles the word, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow."
And the prophet Micah gathers all three into one line: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Now the ladder.
Maimonides, in his code of law, ranked ways of giving. Giving grudgingly sits low. Giving so that neither side knows the other sits high.

teach.h: TOP OF THE LADDER: NO NEED TO ASK AGAIN.
teach.b: At the top: helping someone with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so they never need to ask again.

Here's what makes this shared. These lines live in the Torah, the Prophets and the rabbinic books, the shelf the streams of this block read and argue over. Orthodox and Reform Jews may disagree about why a command binds.
A Humanistic Jew may read Micah without a God who requires anything. The box still gets filled, and the soup still gets carried to the neighbor.

how: Jewish homes and synagogues in different streams keep tzedakah boxes, collect for the poor before holidays, and run volunteer projects; giving is described as justice, not only generosity.

s: tzedakah is just another word for optional charity
some teachers hear tzedek, justice, in it: giving as setting things right.
Simeon the Just named acts of loving-kindness as one of three things the world stands on
with Torah and worship, in the Mishnah.
Maimonides ranked anonymous giving as the very highest
higher still: helping someone so they never need to ask again.

games.q: a neighbor has lost work and is struggling. you have some money to help. on Maimonides' ladder, which way of giving sits at the top?
o: give in secret, so neither of you knows the other.
give a loan, a partnership or a job, so they can stand on their own.
give publicly, so others are inspired to give.
games.why: Maimonides placed at the top the help that makes someone no longer need help: a gift, a loan, a partnership or work.

practice: Let one person or cause come to mind, someone who could use a little of what you have: money, time, or a skill, like cooking or writing a letter for someone who can't.
Choose one gift small enough to give and real enough to matter, and picture where it lands. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if not, hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Shared ethics. Giving, kindness and justice: tzedakah, chesed and tzedek, taught from texts the streams hold in common, however they read them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: giving to those in need, a word some teachers link to tzedek, justice.

carryVoice: Your line: tzedakah: giving that sets the world right. At the top of Maimonides' ladder, no one needs to ask again. Go gently.
